scenes.title: NVD Safety
scenes.text: Night vision device safety. This video covers the limits, hazards, care, and emergency procedures for the AN/PVS-14, for every Soldier who drives, guides, or works around vehicles at night.

scenes.title: Know the Limits
scenes.text: Night vision devices amplify light. They do not turn night into day. The PVS-14 gives you a forty-degree view, poor depth perception, less detail than normal vision, and no color. It needs some light to work, and it cannot see through dense fog, smoke, or dust. Treat it as a tool that helps you see, not a replacement for caution.

scenes.title: Plan for the Light Level
scenes.text: Do plan for the light level. A bright moon gives a clear image. On an overcast, moonless night, the image gets darker and noisier, and you see hazards later. Check the illumination forecast, and adjust speed and routes in the risk assessment. Clouds, terrain shadows, and tree cover can make it darker than the forecast.

scenes.title: Trust the Tube in Dust or Fog
scenes.text: Don't trust the tube in dust, fog, smoke, or heavy rain. They scatter the light and hide vehicles, holes, and ditches until they are close. Slow down, increase your interval, and halt if you cannot see the road. Dust from the vehicle ahead counts too.

scenes.title: Read the Terrain Carefully
scenes.text: Do read the terrain carefully. Shadows and flat light hide ditches, ruts, wires, and drop-offs, and they can look like level ground through a monocular. Scan constantly, and use the assistant driver to confirm what you see. When in doubt, stop, and have someone check it on foot.

scenes.title: Handle the Device With Care
scenes.text: Do handle the device with care. Attach the retention lanyard, keep the lens caps on when the device is not in use, and clean the lenses only with lens paper. Protect it from impact and moisture, and use the daylight training cover when training in daylight.

scenes.title: Manage Batteries
scenes.text: Do manage batteries. Install the correct battery with the right polarity, and always carry a spare. Cold weather drains batteries faster. Remove the battery for storage, and turn in used batteries according to your unit SOP.

scenes.title: Account for Sensitive Items
scenes.text: The PVS-14 is a sensitive item. Sign it out and in, check the serial number, and account for it at every halt and at the end of the mission. A lost device means an immediate search and a serious report. Use the lanyard every time the device leaves its case.

scenes.title: Protect Your Night Vision
scenes.text: Do protect your night vision. Your unaided eye needs thirty minutes or more to fully adapt to the dark, and one flash of white light can undo it. Keep the cab dark, use filtered light, and keep your unaided eye ready in case the device fails.

scenes.title: Device Fails While Driving
scenes.text: If the device fails while you are driving, hold the wheel steady and slow down. Tell the crew, use your unaided eye and the assistant driver, and pull off and stop where it is safe. Troubleshoot only after the vehicle is stopped. Brief this drill before every NVD mission, so the whole crew knows it.

scenes.title: Manage Strain and Fatigue
scenes.text: Do manage physical strain. A helmet-mounted device loads your neck, and long hours on NVDs cause eye fatigue and headaches. Use a counterweight if issued, balance the mount, take breaks, and follow the driver rest plan. After you take the device off, give your eyes a moment before you drive unaided.

scenes.title: Forget IR Discipline
scenes.text: Don't forget IR discipline. The built-in IR illuminator and IR lights are invisible to the naked eye, but anyone with night vision, including the enemy, can see them from far away. Use IR only as your unit SOP and the tactical situation allow. Check that the IR switch is off when you don't need it.

scenes.title: Leaders: Manage the Risk
scenes.text: Leaders, manage the risk. Complete the deliberate risk assessment on DD Form 2977. Set go and no-go criteria for illumination and weather. Confirm every driver is NVD qualified, and check every device before the mission. And remember: anyone in the crew can call a halt when conditions become unsafe.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.text: To recap. Know the limits, plan for the light level, and slow down for dust, fog, and dark terrain. Care for the device and its batteries, and account for it at all times. Protect your night vision, know what to do if the device fails, manage fatigue, keep IR discipline, and manage the risk.

scenes.title: Own the Night Safely
scenes.text: Own the night, safely. Verify these procedures against TC 21-305-2, AR 600-55, the AN/PVS-14 operator manual, and your unit SOP.
